abstract: Abstract Objectives Anti-PL12 autoantibodies are targeted against alanyl-tRNA synthetase, a cytosolic enzyme which plays a vital role in protein synthesis. Clinically, such antibodies are strongly associated with interstitial lung disease and confer a poor prognosis. To better understand their molecular composition, anti-PL12 immunoglobulin variable region subfamily expression and their mutational signatures were analysed by mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics to provide insights into personalized molecular diagnosis. Methods Patients with anti-PL12 autoantibodies were identified from routine myositis immunoblots. Serum anti-PL12 IgG autoantibodies were then purified from specific anti-PL12 precipitins using conventional counter-immunoelectrophoresis. Immunoglobulin (Ig) heavy and light-chains were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE), digested by enzymes and profiled by MS sequencing for immunoglobulin variable region (IgV) subfamily usage and somatic hypermutation analysis. Results Ten patients were identified; seven females and three males with an average age of 65 years. All had lung disease, while two had concurrent myositis. MS sequencing of precipitating anti-PL12 IgGs revealed an oligoclonal repertoire with shared expression of IGHV3-23-encoded heavy chain and IGKV3-20- and IGKV1-27-encoded light chains. Furthermore, shared IgV somatic hypermutations were observed across unrelated patients in both heavy and light chain, in regions likely to be antigen interacting. Conclusion Anti-PL12 autoantibodies among different patients show highly convergent sequences and variable region composition. The inter-individual similarity reveals the evolutionary process towards specific, presumably immuno-dominant, epitopes on PL12 during antigen-driven clonal selection. These unique anti-PL12 autoantibody molecular signatures have the potential to be valuable biomarkers when compared with the simple readout of conventional immunoassays.

Methods
Patient cohort
Patients with a diagnosis of anti-PL12 autoantibody-associated ASyS, as defined by Connors
et al.
criteria [
13
] had sera stored in the immunopathology laboratory as part of a wider myositis biobank. Only sera with precipitin line on K562 cell-line (antigen-rich source from lymphoblastic cells) CIEP extract were included in the study. Patient demographic, clinical and ancillary laboratory data were collected using the Electronic Medical Record. CIEP and MS methodology was performed as previously described [
14
].
Ethics statement
The project was approved by the Southern Adelaide Local Health Network Quality Register Ethics Committee (reference number: 39.034). Deidentified diagnostic residue sera samples were used in this project and a waiver of consent was applied in accordance with the ethics approval by Southern Adelaide Local Health Network Quality Register Ethics Committee (reference number: 39.034).
Anti-PL12 autoantibody purification
Anti-PL12 autoantibodies were purified from serum precipitins reactions between K562 cell extract and serum by a modified Ouchterlony technique [
15
]. Briefly, double diffusion was performed in 1% agarose (SeaKem, Lonza, MD, USA) in a phosphate buffered saline buffer of pH 7.4 at 37°C for 48 h. To ensure specificity, four healthy donors in addition to patients were included, all of whom had absent precipitin lines.
Precipitins were excised, washed extensively in distilled water and solubilized using 1% SDS by boiling at 95°C for 5 min, and immunoglobulins (Igs) fractionated by reduced Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (criterion stain-free TGX gels; Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA).
Mass spectrometry sequencing
In-gel tryptic digests were performed on the 50 kDa H-chain and 25 kDa L-chain bands and peptides analysed with a Dionex Ultimate 3000 UPLC coupled with a Thermo, Exploris 480 tandem mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). An inhouse analytical column created from 75 µm inner diameter fused silica capillary with an integrated pulled tip emitter, packed with 1.9 µm ReproSil-Pur C18 beads (Dr Maisch, Ammerbuch, Germany) to 25 cm, coupled with an inhouse packed trap column made from 300 µm inner diameter fused silica capillary, packed with 1.9 µm ReproSil-Pur C18 beads to 5 mm were used. Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid in water and mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. For each injection, 1 µg peptides were loaded and separated using a 60 min gradient from 3% to 31% mobile phase B, followed by a 25 min washing and equilibration gradient. Samples were analysed using data-dependent acquisition utilizing a 2 s cycle time instrument method. Briefly, ms1 scans were performed using an orbitrap resolution of 60 000 and a scan range from 350 m/z to 1200 m/z. A normalized automatic gain control (AGC) target of 3 × 10
6
with auto maximum injection time mode used. An intensity threshold of 3e5 and dynamic exclusion time of 10 s was employed for all data dependent ms2 scans that were acquired at 15 000 resolution, AGC target 1 × 10
5
, 30% normalized collision energy in the higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) cell, with auto maximum injection time mode used.
Protein sequence data analyses
Peptide sequence analysis was performed by
de novo
sequencing and International ImMunoGeneTics (IMGT) database matching using Peaks studio XPro software (Bioinformatics Solution Inc., Waterloo, ON, Canada). Parameters for database searches, data refinement and Ig variable region subfamily assignments were described previously [
16
].
Mutational analysis and plotting
Alignment was imported from Peaks and parsed in R. To estimate the distance of antigen from individual residues, the crystal structure of germline IGHV3-23/IGKV3-20 (rcsb pdb 5i1c) was used to obtain distances, by setting a hypothetical point 20 Å away from the midpoint of the crystal structures antibody antigen binding interface and then custom Python script was used to calculate residue distances. All plotting was conducted using R version 4.5.
Fig. 1A
was produced with Biorender. For
Fig. 1B and C
, packcircles R package was utilized, and for
Fig. 1D–F
, a custom alignment and graphing script was used.
Statistical analyses
Exploratory analyses were conducted using pairwise comparisons (rstatix R package) with either parametric (
t
-test), non-parametric (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) or categorical (Fisher’s exact test) tests depending on the variable’s distribution.

Rheumatology key messages
Shared IGHV3-23-encoded heavy chain and IGKV3-20- and IGKV1-27-encoded light chains demonstrating oligoclonal repertoire.
Shared IgV mutations in both heavy and light chains suggestive of common antigen interaction.
Introduction
The tRNA synthetase enzymes are responsible for many cytosolic functions including protein chaperoning [
1
]; these enzymes may become antigenic targets for autoantibodies implicated in a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; anti-synthetase syndrome (ASyS). Currently, 11 antisynthetase antibodies have been described against distinct tRNA synthetase enzymes. While the pathogenesis is not completely understood, it is postulated that infections, particularly viral infections may lead to activation of cytosolic tRNA synthetases thus exposing autoantigens and generating antisynthetase antibodies in genetically susceptible individuals [
2
]. Additionally, factors such as occupational exposure to dust, gases and fumes as well as tobacco smoking have been associated with the development of antisynthetase antibodies [
3
].
Anti-PL12 autoantibody, directed against the alanyl-tRNA synthetase complex is one of the less prevalent antisynthetase antibodies, and is associated with progressive interstitial lung disease, often in the absence of myositis. Under-recognition of ASyS as an entity, and often with lack of overt muscle involvement contribute to delays in diagnosis [
4
].
Anti-PL12 autoantibodies, like other antisynthetase antibodies, frequently show characteristic cytoplasmic staining on anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing, which may prompt a confirmatory myositis immunoblot (MIB) assay. While line immunoblot provides rapid semi-quantitative assessment, both false-positive and false-negatives may be seen. The gold standard counter immunoelectrophoresis (CIEP) is performed by a limited number of diagnostic laboratories due to efficiency constraints and expertise. Immunoprecipitation using radiolabelled protein and RNA immunoprecipitation remains the most sensitive and specific method of antibody detection but is labour intensive and remains confined to research laboratories [
5
].
Collectively, these immunoassays provide semi-quantitative, or qualitative information on the presence of anti-PL12 autoantibody. Given variations in detectable levels of these autoantibodies and disease phenotype [
6
,
7
], further biomarkers are urgently required.
Immunoglobulins/antibodies may show progressive and dynamic changes in response to ongoing disease activity, or in response to treatment. Mass spectrometry (MS) is a powerful method to identify and characterize the immunoglobulin at a protein level, thereby providing crucial insight into personalized medicine by identifying diagnosis and prognosis biomarkers and therapeutic targets [
8
,
9
]. This technology evaluates variable regions of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGHV) and light chain (IGLV) and has potential utility in clinical practice. For example, in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, IGHV5-51 and IGHV1-69 are associated with poor prognoses [
10
] while point mutations in IGLV3-21*01 stimulate autonomous B-cell receptor signalling [
11
]. Moreover, a restricted antibody repertoire was reported in immunodeficient patients compared with healthy subjects [
12
].
To date, this has not been elucidated for anti-PL12 autoantibody. Given the important clinical implications of anti-PL12 autoantibody, characterization of its serum antibody repertoire could be invaluable for identifying novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers.
Here, we studied the immunoglobulin composition of anti-PL12 autoantibodies using our efficient in-house proteomic workflow (
Fig. 1A
), hypothesizing that these antibodies show convergent patterns of heavy and light chain subfamily expression consistent with shared pathways of anti-PL12 autoantibody production.

Results
Patient demographics and clinical details
Ten patients with anti-PL12 autoantibodies were studied (
Table 1
), mean age 65.5 years (range 38–81 years) and female predominance (
n
= 7). Nine patients had concurrent anti-Ro52 antibodies. All patients exhibited interstitial lung disease phenotypes; two patients (20%) additionally had histologically confirmed myositis and five had symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis. Nine of the 10 patients were on prednisolone and immunosuppressive therapies. Two of the 10 patients had a significant solid organ malignancy: metastatic breast carcinoma (case 1) and thyroid carcinoma (case 3), respectively.

Over a mean follow up of 8 years (range 2–22 years) four deaths occurred (40%); two were attributed to respiratory failure. One patient had progressive decline in respiratory function at 16 years.
Variation in precipitating anti-PL12 autoantibody heavy and light chain variable region subfamilies
MS sequencing of tryptic digests of IgG heavy chains of patients with anti-PL12 autoantibodies revealed an oligoclonal repertoire with shared expression of the IGHV3-23 subfamilies in all sera and minor expression of IGHV1-69, IGHV1-18 or IGHV5-51 subfamilies in some sera (
Fig. 1C
). Light chain sequencing demonstrated kappa light chain restriction in the precipitating PL12 autoantibody repertoire, with dominant subfamily expression of IGKV3-20 in all patients and IGKV1-27 in most patients (
Fig. 1B
). Private antibody light-chain subfamilies were identified in individual subjects (
Fig. 1B
).
Examining for preliminary disease associations, IGHV5-51 (in combination with IGKV1-27) was present in three patients, two of whom had significant malignancy, and the third of whom required supplementary oxygen (case 2). Whilst four of seven subjects with an IGKV1-27 subfamily in their PL12 autoantibody repertoire had an elevated creatine kinase levels (
vs
none of three without), six of seven required corticosteroid (
vs
one of three without), though none of these explored associations reached statistical significance due to small sample size.
Subfamily somatic hypermutation convergence in all subjects
Investigating high confidence
de novo
peptide sequences and their alignment to reference sequences we observed a pattern of highly restricted mutations (
Fig. 1D–F
). We observed mutations in the IGHV3-23 antigen-binding, complementarity determining and antigen exposed, regions to be enriched for positive charged (lysine, K, and arginine, R) residues in the heavy chain complementarity determining region 1 and 2 (HCDR 1 and HCDR2) (
Fig. 1D
). Meanwhile, with IGKV3-20, hydrophobic aromatic residues were favoured, though frequently mutations resulted in highly similar amino acid replacements, sharing broad categories of amino acid function. Overall, a highly convergent set of amino acid changes was observed, with key heavy chain residues showing convergent evolution towards positive changes in the HCDR1, HCDR2 and N-terminus, with similar convergence though with divergence from germline amino acid properties in the light chain residues.
Discussion
We report the first molecular profiling of serum anti-PL12 autoantibodies, providing important insights into their secreted repertoires. MS sequencing of purified anti-PL12 immunoglobulins revealed convergent responses among unrelated individuals. The presence of shared mutations, convergent mutations to specific amino acids, and inversely common regions of low mutation rates suggests that for the dominant antibody subfamilies observed, there are common structural determinants governing their antigen binding. This suggests that specific germline subfamily features are critical to PL-12 autoantibody selection. Given there is acquisition of a convergent set additional likely classical antigen-driven mutations which lead to pathogenicity, germline affinity alone is unlikely to be pathogenic, but may contribute to disease emergence and characteristics. The dominant IGHV3-23-encoded heavy chain and IGKV3-20-encoded light chain have been found previously in sera with anti-Ro60, anti-Ro52 proteomes in primary SS and in sera with anti-dsDNA antibodies from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus [
14
,
16
,
17
]. However, individual Ig variable region subfamily and differences in their mutational profiles were identified between anti-Ro/La, anti-dsDNA and anti-PL12 autoantibodies.
Drawing on the subfamily differences between individuals, we observed an association between malignancy with IGHV5-51, and elevations in creatinine kinase with IGKV1-27 which may reflect disease associated repertoire features. However, these findings are preliminary, in a very small cohort of subjects, and must be evaluated in a significantly larger, prospective cohort to determine the accuracy of these correlates, and whether they could be used as predictive biomarkers. Notably, the association of anti-PL12 autoantibody positivity and malignancy is not clearly established [
18
].
Previous studies have elucidated that some anti-PL12 autoantibodies bind the anti-codon tRNA itself and may therefore bind across the tRNA–RNA synthetase (TRS) complex. We observed remarkably that there was an enrichment of positively charged residues (K, R) as in the HCDR region of IGHV3-23 (
Fig. 1D
), which is typically seen in nucleotide binding domains such as those interacting with tRNA [
19
]. Whilst in the IGKV3-20 light chain, hydrophobic residue mutations were frequently observed (
Fig. 1E
), with aromatic residues known to interact strongly with both nucleotides and protein epitopes. This leads us to hypothesize that charged and hydrophobic interactions may facilitate formation of epitopes which bridge the tRNA–TRS complex.
Given that patients with anti-PL12 autoantibody may not present with the full house of features of ASyS including the typical features of diagnosis can be delayed. Furthermore, unless a MIB is requested, the diagnosis may be overlooked as this autoantibody is not available on the extractable nuclear antigen immunoblot and cytoplasmic pattern on ANA is not specific. On the other hand, interpretation of the anti-PL12 antibody testing on the MIB must be interpreted in the appropriate clinical context, due to false positives because of conformational epitopes [
20
,
21
]. Additionally, the MIB immunoassay is not quantitative and there are no validated biomarkers to monitor disease. In this context, it is possible that our approach of fingerprinting the antibody repertoire to identify distinct antibody mutation sequences could be used as biomarkers not only in diagnosis, but also for monitoring disease progress. These may then enable a more personalized approach to management.
Mass spectrometric sequencing is a powerful approach for identifying Ig subfamilies and mutational profiles. However, heavy/light chain pairing are not able to be determined in oligoclonal populations by bottom-up proteomic approach alone. Moreover, the HCDR3 regions are difficult to identify accurately in oligoclonal populations by bottom-up proteomic approach alone due to the lack of reference databases for this hypervariable region. More precise understanding of antibody specificity, especially identification of HCDR3, may be addressed by pairing proteomic profiling of anti-PL12 antibodies with paired B cell receptor (BCR) nucleotide databases [
22–24
].
Due to the limitation on the relatively small number of patients used and being a single centre, a clear clinical association with anti-PL12 subfamilies is not established from our current study. Although our results indicate a correlation of IGHV5-51 and IGKV1-27 with organ malignancies, the findings need to be confirmed in a larger cohort from different centres presenting different clinical features and improve generalizability. Longitudinal studies of antibody profiles would also be useful, as changes of repertoire may be apparent during treatment intervals. Identification of this may then be used as predictive modelling for disease control or activity.
In summary, this study describes the first sequence-based serum antibody repertoire study for anti-PL12 antibodies in patients with ASyS. Anti-PL12 autoantibodies show a restricted and convergent subfamily usage, consistent with shared epitope recognition and antigen-driven clonal expansion. This information provides specific insights into antibody production in autoimmune diseases and could lead to the development of novel diagnostic biomarkers and identification of targeted therapeutics.
